messages.subject: How is loss to follow-up treated in CFA
parts:
Hi Yves,

sorry for a somewhat naive question. Naive - because I am sure that there is a straight forward answer and I was not able to find it.

I am trying to run CFA to obtain predicted latent variables of cognition following the paper from Gross et al.

Gross, Alden L., et al. "Application of Latent Variable Methods to the Study of Cognitive Decline When Tests Change over Time." Epidemiology 26.6 (2015): 878-887.

 I am following participants for 6 waves. At each wave, I have 8 different cognitive measures. I understood that FIML does not work with ordinal data, so I imputed using AMELIA to have complete data and no item non-response. But what happens to "structural" missing? Of the 4927 people I start with only 1473 make it through all the waves.

So using the simple syntax:

 cfa.out[[i]] <- fit <- cfa(COG.model, data = imp, ordered=c("TM0_1_TE_FAC","TM0_2_TE_FAC","TM2_1_TE_FAC","TM2_2_TE_FAC","TM4_1_TE_FAC","TM4_2_TE_FAC","TM5_1_TE_FAC","TM5_2_TE_FAC","TM6_1_TE_FAC","TM6_2_TE_FAC","BENTON0_FAC","BENTON1_FAC","BENTON2_FAC","BENTON4_FAC","BENTON5_FAC","BENTON6_FAC","BDEP0_1_FAC","BDEP0_2_FAC","BDEP2_1_FAC","BDEP2_2_FAC","BDEP4_1_FAC","BDEP4_2_FAC","BDEP5_1_FAC","BDEP5_2_FAC","BDEP6_1_FAC","BDEP6_2_FAC","MMSTT0_FAC","MMSTT1_FAC","MMSTT2_FAC","MMSTT4_FAC","MMSTT5_FAC","MMSTT6_FAC","COU0_30_FAC","COU1_30_FAC","COU2_30_FAC","COU4_30_FAC","COU5_30_FAC","COU6_30_FAC","ANI0_30_FAC","ANI1_30_FAC","ANI2_30_FAC","ANI4_30_FAC","ANI5_30_FAC","ANI6_30_FAC","FRU0_30_FAC","FRU1_30_FAC","FRU2_30_FAC","FRU4_30_FAC","FRU5_30_FAC","FRU6_30_FAC","VIL0_30_FAC","VIL1_30_FAC","VIL2_30_FAC","VIL4_30_FAC","VIL5_30_FAC","VIL6_30_FAC"), estimator="WLSMV" ,link="logit")

leaves me with output that only uses 1473 individuals. Is it possible to retain all individuals?

                                                Used       Total
  Number of observations                          1473        4927


I mean: someone who was only there for 2 waves should not be excluded, he/she should simply not get a summary score of cognition beyond wave 2.

Thanks.
Stefan

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: How is loss to follow-up treated in CFA
parts: what happens to "structural" missing? Of the 4927 people I start with only 1473 make it through all the waves.
I mean: someone who was only there for 2 waves should not be excluded, he/she should simply not get a summary score of cognition beyond wave 2.

This is a discussion I've had before without reaching a firm conclusion, but I'll share my perspective.  Because this is not specific to lavaan, you might see what people on SEMNET have to say.

The analysis is agnostic about these "structural missing" cases, so I think your imputation model should be specified the same way.  If you fill in best-guesses for all holes in your data (whether they are supposed to be missing or not), then the parameter estimates should not be biased by including the estimated missing values for people who "shouldn't" have observed values.  The goal of multiple imputation is not to make inferences about those imputed values; it is just to have unbiased point and SE estimates of the model parameters.  Multiple imputation is asymptotically equivalent to FIML (i.e., they give you the same answer when you use an infinite number of imputations and the imputation model matches the analysis model).  So although FIML is more aesthetically pleasing because it "handles" the missingness by ignoring it (i.e., maximizing the likelihood of available data with respect to only the associated parameters), multiple imputation should give you the same unbiased results that FIML would have (with additional Monte Carlo variance). 

This analogy might make you more comfortable.  Rubin (inventor of multiple imputation) described estimation of causal effects as a missing data problem.  When we estimate the mean difference between a treatment and control group, we want to know the effect of the treatment condition.  That value would in reality be the difference between the treatment-group's response to the treatment condition and the (same) treatment-group's response to the control condition.  (Or equivalently, the difference between the control-group's response to the treatment condition and the (same) control-group's response to the control condition.)  We are missing the information about:
  1. what the treatment group would have scored if they had been in the control group
  2. what the control group would have scored if they had been in the treatment group
Because randomization makes the treatment and control groups statistically equivalent (on average), we use the control group's observed mean as a proxy/estimate of the missing mean of (1), and we use the treatment group's observed mean as a proxy/estimate of the missing mean of (2).  The fact that it is not possible to observe the treatment (or control) group in both the treatment and control conditions makes (1) and (2) "structural" missing values in the same sense you used it in your post.  It doesn't matter whether the unobserved cases past Wave 2 were not supposed to be measured -- you can think of the imputed values as proxies of values you might have observed in a hypothetical (even if impossible) situation (counterfactuals, in Rubin's vocabulary), and those imputed values serve no other purpose than to allow you to obtain unbiased point and SE estimates.  If your goal is to estimate factor scores (which are indeterminate, so I wouldn't recommend doing so in general), then you can calculate those estimates and simply ignore the ones it doesn't make sense to interpret.

Terry
